strengths: Reactivating dormant text conditioning: While prior diffusion-based monocular depth estimation methods (e.g., Marigold) discard or zero-out text conditioning in Stable Diffusion, this work demonstrates that retaining and exploiting language descriptions activates the rich geometric and spatial layout priors embedded during large-scale text-to-image pre-training.

Diffusion trajectory and convergence benefits: The paper presents compelling empirical evidence showing that language guidance accelerates training convergence and reduces required reverse denoising steps at inference (converging in ~10 steps vs. ~25 steps for Marigold, as shown in Figure 8 and Table 4).

Thorough diagnostic analyses: The paper provides targeted experiments demonstrating the utility of language conditioning, including evaluating depth on small/occluded objects segmented via panoptic masks (Table 2), interactive controllable depth refinement (Figure 6), sensitivity to prompt templates (Table 3), and fallbacks when explicit captions are unavailable (Table 5).
weaknesses: Marginal quantitative improvements on standard benchmarks: As shown in Table 1, the overall metric gains over baseline Marigold are quite small across datasets (e.g., NYUv2 δ1 improves from 95.9% to 96.0% and AbsRel from 6.0% to 5.9%; KITTI AbsRel from 10.5% to 10.4%). The numerical impact on global benchmarks is modest.

Computational overhead and reliance on vision-language models: The system requires descriptive captions for inference. Generating descriptions via LLaVA v1.6 adds substantial latency (~3.6 seconds per image on an RTX 3090, as noted in Section B.2), which negates the latency gains achieved by reducing diffusion denoising steps. Relying on fixed templates (Table 5) causes performance to revert roughly to baseline Marigold.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The framework directly follows Marigold's training and inference formulation, with the primary difference being the inclusion of VLM-generated text prompts into the cross-attention layers of Stable Diffusion's U-Net. The core technical contribution is largely empirical.

Sensitivity to caption noise and hallucinations: As acknowledged in Figure 9, off-the-shelf VLMs are prone to hallucination or inaccurate spatial descriptions, which can mislead the depth prediction geometry.

strengths: Intuitive motivation: Pretrained text-to-image diffusion backbones (like Stable Diffusion) contain cross-attention modules natively aligned with language. Re-enabling text conditioning for monocular depth estimation rather than zeroing it out or discarding it is a natural and well-motivated concept.

Accelerated inference diffusion trajectory: The analysis in Figure 8 and Table 4 shows that conditioning on language allows the reverse diffusion process to reach convergence in roughly 10 DDIM steps compared to 25 steps for Marigold.

Targeted perception and controllability: Evaluating depth accuracy on small instances using MaskDINO segmentation masks (Table 2) and demonstrating controllable depth refinement via prompt editing (Figure 6) are compelling analyses showing how language can guide depth estimation in subtle or occluded regions.
Comprehensive supplementary material: The paper provides extensive ablations on text prompt templates, prompt phrasing variations, and convergence characteristics.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The proposed framework is essentially the Marigold architecture (Ke et al., 2023) where the frozen CLIP text encoder is populated with captions produced by an off-the-shelf vision-language model (LLaVA-v1.6) rather than empty tokens. The modeling contribution over existing diffusion-based depth estimators is relatively incremental.

Marginal quantitative improvements on standard benchmarks: As shown in Table 1, the improvements over Marigold at full iteration counts are very subtle across benchmarks (e.g., NYUv2 AbsRel 5.9% vs. 6.0%; KITTI AbsRel 10.4% vs. 10.5%; ETH3D δ1 95.8% vs. 95.1%). Given natural benchmark variance, the overall numerical gain from adding dense language captions is quite modest.

High computational and latency overhead at inference: Although diffusion steps are reduced from 25 to 10, the pipeline requires running an MLLM (LLaVA v1.6) to generate image descriptions. According to Supplementary Section B.2, generating a single caption takes ~3.6s on an RTX 3090, which significantly offsets the inference speedup gained from fewer DDIM steps.

Template prompts yield comparable performance to detailed captions: In Table 5, generic template prompts (e.g., Template C, Template I) yield metrics virtually identical to the actual generated image captions (e.g., NYUv2 δ1 95.8-95.9 vs. 96.0; ETH3D AbsRel 6.4-6.6 vs. 6.5). This raises questions as to how much the model truly leverages detailed scene semantics versus benefiting from general conditioning noise modulation during training.

Vulnerability to MLLM hallucination: As illustrated in the failure cases (Figure 9), incorrect or hallucinated descriptions directly corrupt the depth prediction geometry, introducing an error compounding vulnerability from the VLM to the geometric estimator.

strengths: The motivation of investigating whether the language prior preserved in pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models can assist dense geometric estimation is conceptually interesting and intuitively appealing.

The paper is generally well-structured, clear in its exposition, and accompanied by comprehensive supplementary details including prompt designs, training hyperparameters, and qualitative examples across diverse indoor/outdoor scenes.

The exploration of language-guided region control (Figure 6) and the analysis on smaller segmented regions (Table 2) provide interesting qualitative and diagnostic insights into how text conditioning interacts with the visual representation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The proposed framework directly follows Marigold (Ke et al., 2023) by fine-tuning Stable Diffusion v2 for monocular depth estimation, with the only technical difference being that the pre-existing cross-attention conditioning is fed CLIP text embeddings generated by LLaVA rather than null tokens. There are no new architectures, loss formulations, or conditioning mechanisms proposed.

Marginal empirical gains: Compared to Marigold, the quantitative performance gains across zero-shot benchmarks in Table 1 are marginal (e.g., NYUv2 δ1 improves from 95.9% to 96.0% and AbsRel from 6.0% to 5.9%; on KITTI, δ1 is 90.3% vs. 90.4% reported by Marigold). Given the stochastic nature of diffusion sampling, these differences are within standard variance and do not demonstrate a compelling quantitative advantage.

Significant computational overhead and circular dependency: In practice, monocular depth estimation expects a single RGB image as input. By requiring an off-the-shelf vision-language model (LLaVA v1.6) during inference, the pipeline adds ~3.6 seconds per image on an RTX 3090 just for text caption generation. Furthermore, relying on a 2D VLM undermines the claim that language resolves 2D visual ambiguities (e.g., occlusion, small objects, lighting), because the VLM derives its text strictly from the same ambiguous 2D image.

Weak evidence for the role of detailed semantics: In Table 5 (Template prompt comparison), using generic, non-informative template prompts or even 'An image' yields results virtually indistinguishable from detailed LLaVA descriptions (e.g., NYUv2 δ1 of 95.7–95.8 vs. 95.9–96.0; KITTI δ1 of 89.8–89.9 vs. 90.3). This suggests that the model is barely utilizing the descriptive semantic content, and that any marginal difference may stem from generic network regularisation rather than meaningful geometric guidance from text.

Unclear and imprecise theoretical claims: The claim that 'language prior serves as a good initialization of diffusion trajectory' is technically inaccurate, as the reverse diffusion process is initialized from pure isotropic Gaussian noise z_T ~ N(0, I), not from text tokens. The explanation for why text conditioning should accelerate sampling convergence lacks formal grounding.

strengths: Intuitive motivation: Text-to-image diffusion models like Stable Diffusion are originally pre-trained on text-image pairs. Discarding the text prompt entirely (as done in Marigold) discards potential semantic and spatial priors embedded in the cross-attention layers.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple diffusion depth estimators: The empirical study assesses three distinct diffusion-based frameworks (Marigold, Lotus-D/G, and E2E-FT) across five standard benchmark datasets (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, DIODE).

Analysis of sampling and convergence dynamics: The paper demonstrates that language conditioning can provide regularizing constraints that accelerate training convergence and reduce required DDIM sampling steps (Table 4 and Figures 7-8).
weaknesses: Very limited technical novelty: The proposed framework does not introduce new architectural components, fusion mechanisms, or training objectives. It simply activates the existing, native CLIP text conditioning pathway of the pretrained Stable Diffusion backbone and feeds in captions generated by an off-the-shelf VLM (LLaVA/InternVL3).

Marginal quantitative improvements: The metric gains across almost all benchmarks are very modest (often within 0.2–0.8% in $\delta_1$ and 0.1–0.4 in AbsRel, e.g., on NYUv2 from 95.7 to 95.9 for Marigold). Given that no standard deviations or multiple random seed trials are reported, it is difficult to determine whether these gains are statistically significant.

Substantial inference overhead: Generating descriptive captions requires running an external Vision-Language Model (e.g., LLaVA v1.6 or InternVL3-8B). As acknowledged in the supplementary material, generating a caption takes ~3.6 seconds on an RTX 3090, which dramatically dwarfs the inference latency of the depth estimator itself and renders real-time or robotic applications impractical unless captions are pre-existing.

Vulnerability to VLM hallucination: While Figure 9 shows that incorrect text degrades the depth estimation, there is no quantitative analysis or robust mechanism proposed to detect or mitigate VLM hallucinations, which are common for intricate or occluded objects.

Missing comparisons with existing language-guided depth estimators: Although the paper references methods integrating language for depth estimation (e.g., WorDepth [76], RSA [77]), direct experimental comparisons against these language-assisted depth methods are missing.

strengths: Clear and intuitive motivation: While recent diffusion-based monocular depth estimators (e.g., Marigold, Lotus) repurpose pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models by conditioning solely on the input image and dropping text, this work observes that language descriptions can reduce the 3D solution space and resolve visual ambiguities (such as repetitive textures and small/occluded objects).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate the proposed strategy across three distinct diffusion-based depth architectures (Marigold, Lotus-D/G, and E2E-FT) and benchmark them across five standard zero-shot datasets (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, DIODE).

Insightful analysis of convergence and denoising steps: The analysis in Section 4 and Table 4 demonstrates that text conditioning allows the reverse diffusion trajectory to converge in fewer steps (e.g., 10 steps vs. 25 steps for Marigold), which is valuable given the inference latency challenges of diffusion models.

Targeted analysis on challenging regions: The evaluation on small segmentation masks (Table 2) and the iterative refinement qualitative examples (Figure 6) provide clear evidence that textual cues specifically aid regions that are typically ambiguous or neglected in purely visual estimation.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic and technical novelty: The core implementation consists of generating image captions with an off-the-shelf VLM (LLaVA v1.6 or InternVL3-8B) and feeding the resulting embeddings through the pre-existing CLIP text encoder into Stable Diffusion's cross-attention layers. No new architecture, cross-modal alignment mechanism, or training loss is proposed.

Significant computational overhead at inference: Requiring a large vision-language model (e.g., InternVL3-8B) to generate a caption for every test image substantially increases total inference latency, memory consumption, and system complexity, which hinders applicability in real-time or resource-constrained settings (e.g., robotics).

Modest quantitative improvements: Although the performance gains over the baseline models are consistent across datasets, the absolute margins are relatively small (e.g., on NYUv2, delta_1 improves by only 0.2% for Marigold and Lotus-D; on KITTI, AbsRel improves by 0.3%).

Lack of systematic quantification regarding caption noise and hallucinations: As demonstrated qualitatively in Figure 9, incorrect text can mislead depth predictions. However, the paper lacks a systematic benchmark or sensitivity curve evaluating how varying levels of caption error, missing objects, or VLM hallucinations impact estimation accuracy.

Minor presentation inconsistency: In the supplementary material (captions of Figures 10 and 11), the method is referred to as 'PriorDiffusion' rather than 'Iris', which appears to be an uncorrected placeholder from an earlier draft.

strengths: Intuitive and natural formulation: Diffusion-based monocular depth estimators (e.g., Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) build upon pre-trained text-to-image foundation models (Stable Diffusion) but historically dropped or bypassed the text conditioning path. Exploring whether utilizing VLM-generated language descriptions can re-engage these pre-trained spatial/semantic priors is well-motivated and answers an interesting empirical question.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed strategy is validated across three distinct diffusion-based depth frameworks (Marigold, Lotus-D/G, E2E-FT) and evaluated zero-shot across five standard benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, DIODE).

Detailed analyses and ablations: The manuscript provides insightful targeted experiments, including evaluation on small objects using panoptic masks (Table 2), analysis of denoising step convergence (Figure 8, Table 4), sensitivity to prompt wording (Table 3), template-only inference (Table 5), and the effect of misleading textual cues (Figure 9).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The core contribution is largely an empirical study. Stable Diffusion inherently contains cross-attention layers for text conditioning; rather than proposing a novel architecture, conditioning mechanism, or training objective, the paper simply passes VLM-generated image captions into the existing CLIP text encoder of standard diffusion pipelines.

Modest quantitative improvements: Across the main benchmarks in Table 1, the performance improvements over the respective re-implemented baselines are generally incremental (e.g., for Marigold on NYUv2, AbsRel improves from 6.1 to 5.9 and delta1 from 95.7% to 95.9%; on KITTI, AbsRel from 10.7 to 10.4). Given standard evaluation variance in zero-shot transfer, several gains are borderline marginal.

Substantial inference latency and computational overhead: Generating captions using an off-the-shelf vision-language model (e.g., LLaVA v1.6 or InternVL3-8B) introduces significant computational and memory cost. The supplementary material notes that generating a single caption took ~3.6s on an RTX 3090, which undermines the practical efficiency of monocular depth estimation in time-critical applications such as robotics or autonomous driving.

Presentation consistency: In the captions of Figure 10 and Figure 11 in the supplementary material, the method is referred to as 'our PriorDiffusion' rather than 'Iris' or 'Marigold + Text', suggesting leftover text from a previous draft.
